utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of Mico Stanisic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Ms. Tatjana Savic, and Ms. Jessica Lacey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, and Igor Pantelic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've got a couple of administrative matters to raise. It's really one, in fact. We received an e-mail yesterday - I don't know whether Your Honours were informed about the correspondence which was copied certainly to the Registry - that the witness would be fit to testify on Monday. Unfortunately, we received another e-mail today from VWS, also copied, I think, to the Registry, which says that, in fact, the witness is not as in good shape as had been anticipated. He is still receiving intravenous antibiotics. His leg is still apparently not properly recovered. And so it looks like his medication and therapy are going to continue into Monday. Which makes it unlikely, we feel, that he'll be able to give evidence on Monday. Our suggestion is that we reverse the order that was suggested yesterday, deal with the Status Conference on Monday and hope that the witness will be fit to give evidence on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: When we had suggested Wednesday, it was to allow sufficient preparation in advance of the conference. I expect that your suggestion takes into consideration the -- well, assumes that the parties would be prepared for Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I think -- can I say this - and, of course, the Defence can make their representations - I think the real matter, the gravamen, of the Status Conference will be to arrive at a date when the Defence case will be expected to start and when Your Honours will order the 65 ter list. I mean, that's, I think, what everybody needs to know before we break. I've got a couple of other short matters to raise. I will send the list to the Legal Officers tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could we hear from the Defence as to their disposition about moving the -- advancing the Status Conference from Wednesday to Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it is convenient with the Trial Chamber, we agree with this proposal submitted by Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we'll adapt to these changes and try to sufficiently prepare. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner, there was something else you had to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Well, I don't think so, Your Honour. I think that was it. I said "a couple of short matters," but, of course, I suppose, the two are connected. I would, however, just mention one other outstanding motion leaving aside Witness 191 and that's the motion that we filed some time ago about documents that have been MFI'd. The reason is, obviously, before we close our case, we'll have to deal with any further documents that have been MFI'd during the proceedings and which were not covered in our bar table motion. We left those separately, because we felt they came into a separate category. And so it would help enormously if we knew Your Honours' ruling on the earlier application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I can say that that's in its final stages of preparation. Thank you. So the witness is -- is the witness ready to be brought in?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he is. Your Honours, just before he comes in. Your Honours will recall yesterday I mentioned that he had attached to his original witness statement, and indeed gave evidence about in Brdjanin and Stakic, photographs that he took at Trnopolje. They're the only record, as it were, the live record, other than the film that one sees and which I'm going to show him from ITN of what was happening at Trnopolje camp. And, additionally, he drew what Your Honours may feel was a very helpful sketch plan. He's the major witness to talk about Trnopolje. They're not on the 65 ter as I explained yesterday. Until I was preparing for the witness late on, I hadn't appreciated that. I thought there was no point in writing a motion, but my application still would be to be able to use the sketch plan and the photographs with him today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, when you say to use them, just to use them not exhibit them?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, exhibit them, Your Honours. When I say "use," I mean exhibit. And there's no point in the photographs being shown and the plan being used and not being exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So are you making that application now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I mentioned it yesterday, Your Honour. I'm making the application now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Could we -- is the -- does the Defence have a position on this application that's now live? You were alerted to it -- we were all alerted to it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let us leave aside for a moment the fact that the OTP announces this is the last witness who can address the issues. The OTP has been in the possession of these documents, this evidence. They knew about it when they put forward the name of this witness to testify about adjudicated facts. That was in their initial motion in April this year. Meaning the Prosecutor never provided a sound reason for submitting this now. They are submitting this motion a day before the appearance of this witness. Therefore, we believe that this reason is not sufficient, just saying the witness will mostly be talking about Trnopolje. The Defence had to be given notice of this much earlier on, when the witness's name was placed on the list, when the 65 ter proposal was first tabled, the addenda that were proposed. Or at least as soon as the OTP decided who would be a viva voce witness and who would be appearing pursuant to 92 bis. And that is the reason we oppose this motion by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. -- before I hear from Mr. Cvijetic, Mr. Krgovic, moving from the realm of "ought" in which case there's probably likely to be no dispute, how are you embarrassed by this late notice, in terms of the cross-examination that you would have of this witness? I think that that is the crucial question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the fact is we can't examine these witnesses. We didn't have the facts, we didn't check the facts on the ground. There are quite a number of statements after the disclosure last night, the announcement by the OTP. We tried to go through all the witness statements about these photographs, how they were taken, when the prints were made, the whole story, but we simply didn't have the time to check the entire set of photographs. And that's our problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, could I hear from Mr. Cvijetic --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... oh, I see, yes, you didn't hear, because you asked Mr. Krgovic. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic, the same question that I asked Mr. Krgovic, the last question, how are you embarrassed in your being able to defend your client in the light of this late disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to join my colleague, my learned friend Mr. Krgovic on this. This is a relevant witness to the Zupljanin Defence. The position that he has put forward is a joint position by both Defence teams. His is the more relevant opinion because he will probably be asking more questions of this witness. I wonder, as a matter of fact, if we can shall be asking this witness any questions whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... [Previous translation continues] ... can I just say this. Of course, I accept that I should have prepared this witness much earlier than I was able to do and that I would have then realized that. I -- as it so happens, I only had the opportunity - for various reasons which I won't trouble Your Honours with - to prepare him yesterday. Your Honours, there's only one statement made by the witness. The plans are attached to that statement. The photographs, two of them, in fact, you can see on the video which everybody in this court has seen, but the remainder are also relevant. They were disclosed to the Defence in 2006. One of the very first disclosures that we sent out. For the life of me, and I don't think Mr. Krgovic can really say how is he prejudiced. It not that they directly implicate his client in that they're photographs of his client at the camp or anything like that. But, as I say, this is the last witness you're going to hear about Trnopolje. He is the one who is able to describe in complete detail what was happening and what the camp was like. And I think that Your Honours would be assisted by seeing the photographs and the plan and, of course, them being made an exhibit. It's Your Honours' task to have the best possible evidence in front of you, and this is it. And we would suggest, absent any real prejudice that can be shown to the Defence, Your Honours should allow us to lead that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It is of the view of the Trial Chamber that this application -- the explanation given by the Prosecution in support of this application does not show that they have exercised due diligence nor is there sufficiently good cause shown for the admission of this new evidence, and, therefore, we deny the motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I simply want to say this. This is -- I -- I don't know how many times Your Honours have talked about due diligence. Your Honours, I repeat, and I'm not seeking to make you alter your ruling, but it is our submission that Your Honours should have the best evidence available before you, and unless there's a good reason, other than punishing the Prosecution, then Your Honours should accede to these applications. And that's all I want to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is the witness ready to be brought in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. Would you please read the solemn declaration on the card that the usher is handing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And would you confirm that are you hearing me in a language that you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would begin by pointing out to you that the solemn declaration that you have just made impose upon you an obligation to give truthful testimony to the Tribunal. And your -- should you give false or misleading testimony, the Tribunal is empowered to impose the penalties for perjury under the authority of the Statute which constitutes this Tribunal. Would you begin by telling us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Idriz Merdzanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What is your date of birth, and what is your ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on 2nd of January, 1959, and I'm a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is or was your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a doctor. And I'm still a doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you testified previously before this Tribunal or before any of the courts in the former -- the countries that comprise the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified before this Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I testified in court, but I have never testified before the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I would briefly indicate to you the procedure in the trials before this Tribunal, which are not radically different from procedures elsewhere. Namely, that you have been called as a witness, and the side calling you begins. In this case, it's the Prosecution. Then the side opposite would have questions in cross-examination. The Prosecution would have a right to ask questions arising out of what has come up in cross-examination. And the Bench itself may at any stage ask questions of you by way of clarification. It is expected, from what has been reported to us by counsel, that your testimony would be completed before the Court rises at 7.00 this evening. The -- the Court's day is divided into sessions of 90 minutes, which allows for the tapes that record the proceedings to be changed, and that also allows for the convenience of yourself, counsel, the Bench, and the support staff. But notwithstanding those set breaks that I have indicated, if at any time you need to take a break, if you indicate it to us, we will, of course, accommodate you. And I would invite Ms. Korner to begin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doctor, let me start, first of all, with your testifying history, as it were. It was interpreted to us a moment ago that you testified in court but you've never testified before the ICTY. So let's just clarify that. It's right, isn't it, that you gave evidence in the case against Milomir Stakic in - let me just get the date - September 2002?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I understood the former Yugoslavia to mean that I testified somewhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I did testify before this Court in relation to the events that happened during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you testified, as I say, in September 2002, in the case against Stakic. And then in November of the same year, in the case against Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think you've got also probably rare experience of giving evidence in the High Court in London in a libel action that arose out of the report that Penny Marshall, the ITN reporter, made of what happened at Trnopolje. And in respect, particularly, of whether or not the fence that was shown in the video which we'll look at later was actually there or not. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's right. In principle it was about the existence or the non-existence of that fence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And additionally you then -- you also made a statement in August of 2000 to an Office of the Prosecutor investigator. And during the course of taking that statement, you drew various diagrams of Trnopolje and you also provided copies of photographs that had been taken by you or someone who was in Trnopolje with you, Azra Blazevic, of the conditions, including the condition of the room in which interrogations had taken place. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. First of all, Dr. Merdzanic, can I briefly deal with your background, and then we'll move straight to the events of 1992. You, in fact, attended the Faculty of Medicine in Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Between 1978 and 1986. And on completing that part of your education, did you do your compulsory military service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I did. I spent one year in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you, on completion of your military service, get a job in an outpatient clinic as a general practitioner in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: In 1988, a few months after I completed my military service, I got a job in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And eventually were you given a permanent post at the Prijedor Health Centre?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was given a permanent job at the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the Prijedor Health Centre - is this correct? - covered a number of different areas within the municipality of Prijedor, which included Trnopolje, Kozarac, Omarska, and Ljubija. And other places.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's correct. They were outpatient centres which were part of the Prijedor Health Centre. These were field outpatient centres.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And in 1991, did you start working at one of the clinics which was part of the sawmill in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: First I worked in the field outpatient clinic in Trnopolje, and then I was also assigned to a clinic for the employees in the sawmill in Kozarac. During the weekend, we were on duty service, and I did my duty service in Kozarac at the outpatient centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, were you yourself living in Prijedor town?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I lived in Prijedor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Up until the war started in Croatia, was there any difficulty or animosity that you were aware of between the various ethnicities who lived in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Until before the war in the former Yugoslavia, I never noticed any problems between the Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. Either way, I, personally, never had any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you specifically about Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to this line of questioning by Ms. Korner. What's the connection between what the witness knows about Stojan Zupljanin and the adjudicated fact? As he said at the beginning, he was called to testify about specific facts, and the Prosecutor should adhere to that decision by the Trial Chamber from June of this year. This is the fifth or sixth time that the Prosecution is trying to present evidence through the backdoor when witnesses were called to testify about specific facts and their testimony is limited, as is our cross-examination. In this way, the Prosecution wants to introduce evidence through the backdoor, and the Defence does not have any information that the witness would be testifying about these circumstances. This line of questions and this attitude by the Prosecution is in opposition of the decision of the Trial Chamber that the witnesses would be called to testify about specific adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, I gave notice in the proofing note about this witness's knowledge of Stojan Zupljanin, which was sent to the Defence last night at 7.45 and to the Trial Chamber as well. Second, this witness is being called to deal with the attack on Kozarac, which is Adjudicated Fact 844 through to 846, of which I also gave notice, and part of that attack is the negotiations that took place in order to try and prevent that attack with Stojan Zupljanin. So it is not mere -- me merely asking for no good reason about his knowledge of Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, in terms of the proofing note, that couldn't enlarge the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm complaining about the complaint of lack of notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So it's the second part on which you're concentrating.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The proofing note is really neither here nor there in terms of the ruling of the Trial Chamber as to the limits of what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But it is -- it is pertinent to notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, doctor, about that. Could you tell us, did you know Stojan Zupljanin before the war?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew Mr. Zupljanin before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And how did you know him?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I started in Banja Luka at the aero club in -- and I flew aeroplanes that didn't have any engines, and then I moved on to sports aircraft. And a few years before the war, Stojan Zupljanin was also a member of this aero club. So that's where we know each other from, the club in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever have any professional dealings with him as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Professionally or officially, no. We never had any contacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And from your knowledge of him gained through both of you at this flying club, first of all, did you know what ethnicity he was?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Just as now, back then I couldn't tell by the name whether somebody was a Serb or a Croat. I could recognise Bosniaks or Muslims by the names, because those names were a little more different. But before the war, I never differentiated between people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And in all the time you knew him, up until 1992, obviously you -- when you were taken to Trnopolje, did you have -- did you ever hear him express any kind of animosity to those who were not Serb?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I never noticed him to say anything against me or Muslims. I -- I really can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- can we move, please, straight to the time that Prijedor was taken over at the end of April. Were you in Prijedor that day?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I was in Prijedor when the army occupied Prijedor. This was a unit that had returned from the front in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And were you able to get to work that day?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That day I managed to call in to the health centre in Prijedor. They had occupied all the positions in all important places in Prijedor. So in the morning, when I set off to work, I saw that there were check-points where they were checking the cars and identity cards and we realized that Prijedor had been occupied by the army. The health -- there was army in the health centre as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, after that first day, did you carry on going to work at the health centre in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I believe the first day I didn't go at all, and I think that after that, I drove an ambulance to Trnopolje and to Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And were there check-points between Prijedor and Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There were check-points between Prijedor and Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, are you able to remember - and please say so if you can't - who was manning the check-points?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Men in military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we then move, please, to shortly before the events that took place in Kozarac. Did you hear, or were you told, about ultimatums to the inhabitants of Kozarac to surrender their weapons?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I heard that there were negotiations between Prijedor and Kozarac and a delegation from Prijedor and Banja Luka, which included Mr. Zupljanin. And I heard that an ultimatum was given at these negotiations for Kozarac to surrender the weapons and for the police to wear Serbian insignia or surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And did you -- first of all I suppose I'll ask, who did you hear this from? Was it from a member of that delegation?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. I think this was third-hand information from somebody who had heard from somebody who was present at that meeting. I think Sadikovic, who was a doctor, a specialist, he attended that meeting. And I think that the man who I heard it from had heard it from Sadikovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you hear when that ultimatum was to expire? Whether a time and a date was given.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Both the date and the time were specified.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We know that the attack on Kozarac took place on the -- I think it's the 24th of May. Was that the date that was specified?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As far as I heard, the date was the 24th, at noon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before that date and that time, had you done anything in -- in respect of -- of talking to people about the surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I didn't talk to anybody personally about the surrender of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you talk to anybody -- well, first of all, perhaps I can deal with it this way: Did you know someone called Sead Cirkin?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Sead Cirkin is somebody I saw in Kozarac, actually on the suburbs. When I was at the outpatient centre in Kozarac, I was told that there was a man called Sead Cirkin who was an active military personnel and who had a group of people with him who were armed and who were preparing to defend Kozarac. I asked a man to take me to see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: And I talked to him, and I asked him whether things been supplied, whether there were any directions for us on how to behave, what we were to do with the wounded if there were any, and he didn't have any plan. In principle, he told me that I should organise things in the outpatient centre as best we knew. There was no plan for the medical service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. All right. On the day of the attack, what time did the attack start?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I think soon after noon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where were you when the attack started?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I was at the outpatient centre in Kozarac. There was a building there which had several storeys, and that's the building that housed the outpatient centre in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the time the attack started, how did you first become aware that there was an attack going on?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There was shelling everywhere around. Shells fell on the outpatient centre, in the yard. All the cars which were parked there were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't show you any photographs, but can you tell us, was -- the health centre on the outpatient centre, was there any marking to show that it was a hospital or an outpatient ...

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It was the only building. The other houses around were private homes. And everybody knew that this building was a hospital or an outpatient centre in Kozarac. And I believe that there was a red cross on the roof.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Before the shelling started, had there been any warning in the sense of somebody using a loud-hailer saying that if people didn't surrender all their weapons now, they would be shelled? Anything like that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We didn't hear anything at the outpatient centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So once the shelling started, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: What would you do? We hid. We thought first that we could stay on the ground floor, but since all the windows were broken, we hid in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... how many -- roughly how many people were in that outpatient centre at the time the shelling started?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I had a list. There were more than ten of us, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And were there casualties, as a result of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Soon after the shelling, a few people were wounded. One of them was a Serbian soldier called Lugar. He had been shot in the stomach and he was brought to the outpatient centre. Another person was a civilian, but I don't know whether he had a weapon. He was injured in the chest. And then they brought in one other man who was already dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. How long did the shelling go on?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Until the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Other than those people that you've told us about, were there any other injured who, during the course of those -- that shelling which went on until the next morning, came to your clinic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Because of the shelling, not many people could come to the health centre because it was very dangerous to go outside. I recall these two men because they had severe injuries and they couldn't walk on their own. There was another young man, I think. A shrapnel almost cut off his toe. It was hanging just by the skin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you told us you were hiding in the basement. Eventually, did you move out?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The next morning, the shelling was suspended for a short time, for a few hours, so we used this time to move the outpatient centre to the north, in the direction of Mount Kozara, on the outskirts of town. We moved it to a house which was protected by the hill so shells couldn't land there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when you were there, did you receive other casualties?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There were several casualties there. Unfortunately, two of them were very young children.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you try to get any assistance for them?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We didn't have the conditions. There was nothing we could do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doctor, where you were, were there -- where you had moved the clinic to, were there any other part of the authorities at that building?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That building housed the police as well. They had a police car there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you ask them for any kind of assistance?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I tried, by using a radio station which the police used. I introduced myself and I asked them to allow us to take the injured to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did they allow you to do that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And who had you been -- and who were you talking to?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know who it was. But it was the same radio station which was used to agree the surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You may not know the person that you spoke to, but did you understand from what part of the authorities they represented, what part of the authorities they were?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I think it was the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Doctor, I'm sorry to have to ask you about these events again, but, as you know, it's quite important. All right. When they -- when you spoke to somebody, whether it was the army or someone else, what sort of language did they use when they told you that you -- that you couldn't move the children?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I think they said, Just go ahead and die, Balija. We'd kill you soon enough anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Having been refused this assistance, what -- what did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Nothing. I went back. We were in the basement, and the police were up above us, on the first floor. So we just waited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Until the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And how did you come to leave?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The police managed to broker the surrender of Kozarac. They informed us that it had been agreed that the wounded would be the first to be allowed to leave. And then the police and the civilians would also be allowed to leave Kozarac two by two.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So did you make the preparations for -- for leaving?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We organised for the wounded to use those trucks owned by Azra's husband. There was Lugar there, another civilian who had sustained an injury to his chest, and a child whose leg had been shattered. The other, a little girl who was there, had died.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned Azra. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Azra Blasavic was a vet who was there with us throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, before you actually left, did anybody arrive?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? No one arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Where did you -- all right. So you left, did you, in the truck; and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. Azra's husband left with the truck and the wounded. The rest of us went back to the clinic in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. At the clinic in Kozarac, did anyone arrive?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: After that, three uniformed men arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you describe, please, the uniforms that were worn by these men.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Two of them wore camouflage. One of them wore a red beret. And a third, a blue camouflage uniform. The latter was called Skrbic, Dragan Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like to you have a look please, first of all, at Exhibit P1033.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can just blow it up a bit. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said one of them was camouflage with a red beret. Is that the sort uniform and red beret that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, do we have a tab number for this exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's tab ... tab ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I have it as 41. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And now could you have a look, please, at a short clip from a video which is V000-8836, which is tab ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say one of them was wearing blue camouflage. Is that the sort of uniform that you're describing?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Just like that. They all had the same arm-band, I think, on the left arm. The same colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said -- I think that's P -- tab 42. Sorry, P1393.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you say the same arm-bands. Were -- was just the man with the blue camouflage wearing an arm-band or all of them?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: All of them. All the soldiers who came to Kozarac wore one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Doctor, I know you're a bit upset. Would you like to take a break now, or are you happy to carry on for a bit longer?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I'm ready to press on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So these three people arrived in uniform. And what did they do?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The one with the red beret was very nervous. He kept saying we should all be shot. And then they noticed Goga, who wore a name tag on her overcoat. She was a Serb, and they led her across the way from the rest of the group and spoke to her. Dragan Skrbic told us to wait there until she was back. And he was gone for some time. When he was back, he said a truck would be coming along and we were to load all of our things onto that truck and would then be taken away. But that was all he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did a truck arrive?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. We loaded all of our medicine that we had in the clinic onto it. And then we were marched one by one from the clinic to what was virtually a crossing, cross-roads, in Kozarac. We stood there for a short time, waiting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you were marched, is that the cross-roads that's at the end of Kozarac with the -- the junction with the Prijedor road?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. This is a junction within Kozarac itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What could you see happening in the -- in the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: In the town itself, there were very many soldiers. They went into houses; they searched these houses; they tried to get into cars and ignite the engines. Some of them were just standing. As soon as we reached the junction in Kozarac, there were two tanks there. The place was teeming with soldiers, some moving and some stationery.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The tanks that you saw there, what kind of tanks were they? Were you able -- because of your military service were you able to identify them?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Those were military tanks. I'm not sure about the type or make.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Apart from tanks, did you see any other kind of vehicles that belonged to either the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I object to that. I mean, it's leading, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think it is, Your Honours. I'm asking whether he saw any other vehicles that belonged to either the police or the army. I cannot, for the life of me, see why that's leading. He's just described tanks which he said were army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, doctor. Can you answer that? Did you see any other vehicles that were either police or army vehicles?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I can't say with certainty right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's fine. What about damage? You've explained how the place was shelled for effectively nearly 24 hours. What sort of damage had been done by the shelling?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There were branches from trees lying on the ground. Pock marks on the walls of some of the surrounding houses. Holes went through the roofs. Pock marks on the road as well from bits of shrapnel. And shells exploding, leaving holes in the road, some small and some bigger. There was a lot of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We know -- we know that Kozarac had, I think, at least two mosques. Did you see whether they'd been damaged during this?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I wasn't paying attention. Those were further north. I think one is across the road from the house where we were, and I believe it was a sheltered house, but I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's fine. All right. There you are at the cross-roads from Kozarac; where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: After a while, a military jeep arrived. But before they put us into that jeep, a soldier came up to Bahonjic, Nihad, our ambulance driver, and ID'd him. When he showed his ID, the other man took hem away. Right after, the military jeep arrived. We were told to get into it. I simply asked in passing what had become of Nihad Bahonjic and they said they were taking care of him. We headed out in that jeep, left Kozarac, and took a right turn towards Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, what happened to Nihad Bahonjic, who had been taken off by these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We heard shots. I don't know whether that was when they killed him or not. But no one ever saw him again. I don't even know whether his body was ever found.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you go towards Prijedor, and where do you end up?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Basically we got as far as a cafe further down the road on the left-hand side. We took a turn there and stopped. There were many soldiers in that cafe, even high-ranking officers; many of them, in fact. We waited there. We got out of the jeep. Soon a bus arrived full of women and children, coming from Prijedor. There was this one man whose name was Husidic; they led him away. I heard they accused him of being a member of the Green Berets and they wanted to take him away, but his wife was there with two young children and she pleaded with them to let him go. We confirmed that that wasn't true. Then we said that there was a man in the clinic with us, the highest-ranking man, and he was to get on the bus with us. But then they went back for him and took him away to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you learn that he had been taken to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as our team was concerned, when we all stuck together, they took him, Dr. Pasic, and Dr. Mensur Kusuran. They took them to Omarska. They were with us in the clinic. They came to the clinic and took them away at different points in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Sorry, I think we -- it may be me, but there's slight confusion going on. You talked about the man who they were accusing of being a Green Beret. And --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you mean -- did he come with you - as you were going to tell us - to Trnopolje and then was he taken, or was he taken away at that stage?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. He was first released and allowed to get on that bus with us. He arrived with us in Trnopolje, and then they took him from there to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And the doctors that you've named, perhaps you could name then again because it doesn't seem to have gone on to the LiveNote. Who were the two doctors?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Two doctors: Dr. Jusuf Pasic and Dr. Mensur Kusuran.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said they, too, were taken away at different times. Is that, again, from Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: From Trnopolje. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So can we just establish - and I should have asked you earlier - which of you from the clinic had been taken by these armed men to the cafe. Yourself and who else?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... all right. You've told us these soldiers arrived -- or these -- not soldiers. These armed men arrived at your clinic and that they then --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in Kozarac. Then you went to this cross-roads and then you were picked up and taken to the cafe. Who was with you?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: They took us to that cafe in a military jeep. We didn't actually enter there. We were standing by the road. There is another road forking off there, a dirt track not an asphalt road, that leaves the asphalt road at one point and heads out towards Trnopolje. We were all standing there in a group.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And what I'm just trying to get at - and it's my fault; I'm obviously not making myself clear - is when you say "they took us," who did they take? Who were the other people who was take -- who were taken, apart from yourself?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The entire team from Kozarac except for Nihad Bahonjic. Not Nihad Bahonjic. We were all taken together. Azra, the vet; another vet who was there; Dzolagic; Mujo and Babica; Goga, the Serb; a lady named Lejla; Husidic; a wife and husband.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... all right. Had any of you got any weapons of any kind?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, no weapons at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did anybody, of the people who had taken you there, search you to see if you had weapons?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Azra Blazevic was the only one who had a back-pack. The others had nothing at all. I can't remember, but I think perhaps back in Kozarac they checked the back-pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Just before we break, then, eventually, were you taken on this bus to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's right. We got onto the bus, and there were mostly women and children there. From there, we were taken straight to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that probably is a sensible place to break, I mean, because I'm going to deal with Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So we take the break, and we would resume in 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I just ask, does your ruling mean that I can't show him the photographs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, Ms. Korner. Since they not on the 65 ter list and will not be admitted to the 65 ter list, you may show them and confront the witness with them, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, could we now deal with Trnopolje. When you got there that first day, you obviously knew Trnopolje because there was a clinic there. Was there anything to show why you'd been brought there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Not that I noticed. Except there were many soldiers around, many women and children. But that was the extent of what I noticed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there anything to show that this was a place where people were going to be staying? Let's use a neutral word for the time being.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. When you arrived there, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We arrived there by bus, and we stopped on a road that is - how shall I put it? - south or south-west of Prijedor in the direction of Trnopolje, the bus stopped there. And there's a path that takes you to that place. To the right, there was some soldiers standing or sitting, and we headed towards this building, all of the people who were on the bus. There were those of us from the clinic who wore our white coats. Rade Baltic was there wearing civilian clothes. He knew me because he used to be a patient of mine. They said that all of us wearing doctor's coats should go to the clinic in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, I'm going to ask to you look at the photograph, please. And I'm afraid it's a modern photograph, because I can't show you any of the earlier ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up on the screen, please -- just a moment. Let me just check for a moment which is the right one. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, while the photo is coming up. Doctor, when you say "soldiers," "there were many soldiers around," do you mean military or do you mean armoured men in general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Armed men wearing military uniforms. And I think those people used to be civilians before then. One of them recognised me. It was a young lad who was at the airport in Prijedor and so was his father. He was not active-duty military personnel. Those were men who were obviously mobilized for purposes of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually, I'm told -- I'm sorry, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's stick with that one for the moment. Then I can show you one that's closer to the time we're talking about, because it was on our list. Can you indicated there - you will be given a pen by the usher and you're able to draw on the screen - whether we can -- this is -- this was only taken last year, but whether -- where the clinic was. I'm sorry. Stop that. This is an overhead view of Trnopolje as it is, effectively, today. Did it look the same in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And can you indicate, please, by drawing a circle, where exactly the camp was. What buildings were included in what became the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: This is the school building. Should I make a marking here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, could you -- could you mark A so we can -- could you write the letter A as the school building.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: This was the courtyard of the school. The clinic is here. And this is the hall. And what you see here is the local commune building. This was a shop where you could buy construction material. At different times, this area here served different purposes. At some points in time, it belonged to the camp, at some points it didn't. It was like this, roughly speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you mark B by the clinic; and C by the hall.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then the shop, could you mark D.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now I want to deal with this point straight away. When you arrived, you told us there was nothing to indicate this was a place that people were going to be staying in. At any stage, was -- was something put up to show that this was a camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Trnopolje camp was, in a way, a dynamic place, because things kept changing there. It was only at one point in time, just before the journalists came, that Keraterm camp had been disbanded all together, and Omarska to some extent, too. And some of the people there were transferred to Trnopolje, so a temporary fence was built and was soon pulled back down after it appeared on TV all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And we're going to see that fence eventually. Did the fence follow the lines that you've drawn to indicate the area which was the camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where did -- it may be a bit difficult, but can you indicate where the fence was when it was up? If you're finding it too difficult -- I know you did a diagram at the time, doctor, but it would help if you could just indicate --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No problem at all. No problem at all. I can do it on this image. There was already a fence here. The shop that was there already had a fence. And when they set up the fence, they built one from this fence to the end of the hall, and then this area there was also fenced off. That was the only fence that stood for a short time. The others were already in existence. The school had a fence, which was very low; and then there was a fence in front of the clinic, which was also rather low.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you very much, doctor. That's all I'm going to ask you about that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could that be separately exhibited, Your Honour, then, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1770, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Mr. Aleksic wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. Now it's already been given an exhibit number. It might be good that the area that the doctor marked as having a fence should receive a different number so that it's clear. Or maybe it should be marked with a different colour or have the letter F so we would know what's what.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did think about that, but I think it's pretty clear. But, I mean, we could --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doctor, can you -- where you drew that fence which we can see surrounding it, can you just mark the letter F to the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the fence that was in existence before or the one that was constructed?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no, the one that was constructed, please, which you marked for us.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The one that was constructed is this area here. And this area here, on this side. The fence lower down was already in existence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there another colour available that -- although he's already marked it in red, if there's another colour available, if he just follows the same line, perhaps that would ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the constructed fence is this area and this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. All right. And can we just very quickly have a look, please, at a photograph that, as I say, is -- was taken nearer the time. And that's 0 -- sorry, 2483, which is tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 65 ter 2483. Anybody? Is it ... I don't really want -- oh.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doctor, the two buildings there that we can see in the foreground, can you just identify those for us, please.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The one on the right is the school in Trnopolje; and, on the left, in the front you can see the shop, the clinic, the local commune on the first floor, the sports club. And behind it you can see the hall, the hall that was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1771, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, doctor, at what stage -- you arrived towards the end of May, obviously, because it was a couple of days after the shelling. At what stage did Trnopolje become this camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We noticed that more and more women and children arrived each day and that nobody was leaving. The smaller number of men who were there were separated and placed in the school. And eventually, when there were loads of people and you were unable to fit any more in, convoys were organised. And this convoy went from Trnopolje to move these people towards Sarajevo through the territory of Doboj. In principle, already after a few days, since there was army around and there were check-points around, there was no freedom of movement; it was not possible to enter or leave without being checked. So we realized and it became clear to us that it was what became called a camp, or a prison. There was no freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've said that more and more women and children arrived. How were they arriving at the camp at the -- at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: They were most frequently brought in by buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say that it became a camp or a prison. There was no freedom of movement. Were people allowed to leave Trnopolje if they wanted to? For example, yourself. Did you want to stay in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I was not allowed to leave Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about other people? You've told us that people were taken out, convoys were organised. What about the other men who were there, were they allowed to leave?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Only women and children and people over the age of 65, who were not able-bodied, to leave the camp. Those who were able-bodied had to stay. Only very few such people came to Trnopolje. There was something called the mopping up of villages. They would surround a village, and army or police - I don't know who - would enter the village; they would force the people out of their homes; line them up; single out the women, children, and elderly on one side; they would be sent to Trnopolje. Some of these people were killed or are missing. Some were taken to Keraterm. Some to Omarska. And a smaller group of people who either had some connections or somebody helped them, a Serb helped them, were sent to Trnopolje because that was deemed to be the best place for men to be. They allowed men to leave the camp only after the visit by the journalists.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: And one more thing - I'm sorry. Those who came to Trnopolje, those men who came to Trnopolje, were still sometimes called out by name and they would be taken to Omarska or somewhere else or they were beaten. So not everybody who came to Trnopolje was safe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you weren't allowed to leave. There were check-points. What else was preventing you from leaving? Were there guards at this place?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Of course. At the check-points and the drawing that I made previously, there were check-points there guarded by armed men, by guards who had weapons. These guards changed every few weeks, and new people would come every few weeks. Major Kuruzovic, who came a few days after the first days, stayed the same, and a few other people stayed along with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about -- you told us about guards. Were the guards armed?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Of course they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were those personal arms? In other words, rifles or the like, or were there other weapons there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: At the check-points, there were other weapons as well. But it depended on the unit that was there to guard the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And were you -- do you know who these men were? I mean, you say they were uniformed -- or I don't think you say, actually -- you say they were guards. Do you know where they came from?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: One group which rotated more frequently than the others were from the neighbouring villages. But there were others as well who, when they came to rest from the front, would be dispatched there. For a while they all were sent to the front, so some older people were brought in. They were mainly men who had been mobilized, not active, professional military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, sorry, I'm just thinking for a moment. Did you -- there were check-points, you say. Were there any check-points or any armed people within the area of the camp itself?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: In the camp, inside the circle that I drew, there weren't any. Only around.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I then turn, please, to the conditions -- sorry, the convoys that you talked about. How did people leave the camp? In what sort of transport?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We usually heard a day before that a convoy would go the next day. Then reinforcement would arrive. A man called Beric came with them. And then they moved from the camp towards the railway station. They were lined up. And then the women and the children walked along the middle of the street, two by two, and they checked to make sure that there were no men in these groups. If there was somebody who had a good friend who was a Serb, then they would manage to have a man included. And then these people were loaded onto cattle wagons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So this was at the station, was it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. At Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you say you were on cattle wagons. Was there seating in them?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see "temperature" has come up on the screen. Was there seating in "them," I asked, at line 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how full were these cattle wagons?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I replied already. Of course, they tried to get as many people in there as they could.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was the weather like at this time of year?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It was summer down there, so it was very, very hot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's deal with the conditions that were at Trnopolje until the journalists and then the ICRC arrived. Food. Was that supplied by the guards or Major Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There was no organised food distribution. But in the beginning, they allowed the locals from the neighbouring places to bring food to the people in the camp. There was some Serbs who brought food.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You say "in the beginning they allowed locals ..." How long did that go on that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That went on until these locals were forced out of their homes and expelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So how was food provided thereafter?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: At the end of May, the Serbian Red Cross arrived, and we managed to arrange through them to have milk brought in for young children, and they collected money from people who were in the camp and then they bought bread, which they brought in the next day. And then they distributed this bread to the people who had given money for it. At one point -- this was all at different points in time, but at one point they organised sort of a military kitchen. There was a makeshift stove on which it was possible to cook. However, this was nothing for that large number of people. And afterwards, when the International Red Cross arrived, then we had food regularly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And we may as well get the date. When did the International Red Cross arrive?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: In mid-August.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about accommodation? Was there sufficient rooms in the buildings that you've shown us to accommodate these people?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: When they would empty the camp after a convoy would leave, they would start bringing in more and more people, so then space would run out. At one point, some people had to sleep outside on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sanitary facilities - running water, toilets, baths - did they exist?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There were no bathrooms, of course. We only had running water for the first two or three days, but it was dirty so it was cut off. The toilets in the school were soon blocked, so they dug latrines outdoors where you could then use the toilet. They constructed little cubicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Was that sufficient for when the camp was full, before convoys took them off?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Medical supplies. You told us that before you left Kozarac you had taken such medical supplies as you could from the clinic. Were you given more?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. No, that's not correct. I said that we loaded all the medicine from Kozarac on the truck, but they drove off with that. We never saw any of that medicine again. We didn't have any medical supplies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you treat people at the clinic? In -- sorry, in Trnopolje, not in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As best we could, using the supplies that we had at the clinic. We had very limited supplies. Some medicine was left over. We sometimes received things from the locals. And when the International Red Cross arrived, they talked to me and asked me what I needed, so then they would bring things. Dusko Ivic, a doctor, visited the camp, and a man called Mico who was a technician. He was a Serb. And they brought us some powder against lice so those who had lice could use the powder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, what sort of injuries were you treating at your clinic in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As for injuries, they were just injuries sustained during beatings and injuries caused by knives.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When were the beatings taking place? And who was doing the beating?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Most of the beatings in that period before the arrival of the journalists and the arrival of the International Red Cross happened then. Later, they were very rare. Uniformed people would always come. Some of them we knew and some of them we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what would they do?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: They either brought themselves or they would call people out by their names, take them into a room. It was one room where these people were brought. They might have been taken elsewhere as well, but I don't know that, and that's where they were beaten. Afterwards these people were most frequently taken away. A smaller number of them were brought to us to see whether there was anything that we could do for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the room that they were being taken to, where was that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It was in the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, at various stages, were photographs taken of what the room looked like and of some of the beaten people?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. We managed to make a very, very small number of such photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was this a camera that -- that -- that Azra Blazevic had?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was Azra Blazevic's camera. And we hid it in a water tank because there was no water.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, eventually, as we'll see when we watch the video, were you able to smuggle out a film with Penny Marshall and the ITN crew?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: When Penny Marshall visited for the first time, we managed to give her the camera. She wanted to take out the film and return the camera, but we were afraid that they would find it, so we asked her to take it away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, now to have a look at just some of the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, could we have a look at, I think it's tab 20, and the number that it was given, 10611, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What does that show us, Dr. Merdzanic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's the room where the people were beaten. On one occasion, we managed to take a photo so that you could see the blood.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we look, please, at the next one, which I think is the same; it's 10612.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It's the same room from another angle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we look, finally, I think, at two -- sorry. It's 10613. That's, as we'll see, the one that was particularly displayed on the video. Who is that young man?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's Nedjo, who they beat. Nedjo Jakupovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Doctor, if you need to take a break, we will, of course, accommodate you. Should we take a five-minutes' break?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it might be -- well, I -- I'm not -- if I can just show him the next photographs. Well, actually, I don't think I need bother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let me hear from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's all right. We can continue. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, doctor. I'm not going to ask you to look at any more photographs because we'll see those later in the video. These beatings that took place in this room, were people being questioned whilst they were at Trnopolje? Anybody.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I know that some were questioned. And I have no idea why some of the others were beaten. We weren't there. I know about the ones they brought over to us to have a look. But they would always accuse them of something or other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, apart from beatings, were there any deaths as a result of this kind of violence?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember the name; it's somewhere in my statement, the person's name. There were many more of those whom they would first beat and take away somewhere outside the camp to shoot them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know a family called Foric?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, not personally. I do, however, know that one day they were looking for someone named Foric. They took them away, took them down the road to the railway station and killed them there. There were five or six persons involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I saw them being taken away. Azra said that they had killed them, as well as other inmates. I think it was Curkus, on behalf of the Serbian Red Cross, who organised to bury their bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about some people called Murgic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to know how -- what this has to do with adjudicated facts and which particular adjudicated fact this is in relation to, this isolated incident that Ms. Korner is addressing now. I have not been able to establish any links between this and any of the adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just finding it, thank you, Your Honour, if Your Honours require me to answer this. Your Honours, if you look at Adjudicated Fact 1031. On or about the 1st of October, 1992, people were removed from Trnopolje camp on signing an agreement to relinquish all of their material goods - crossed out, in other words - thus the Trnopolje camp was the culmination of the campaign of ethnic cleansing ... since those Muslims and Croats were not killed at Omarska or Keraterm camps but were from Trnopolje ... deported from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Your Honour, in our submission, ethnic cleansing includes killings in camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. But how does this -- how -- how does this -- this enter the particulars of the family to whom -- of whom you're now? Inquiring.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: How does the indicated adjudicated -- disputed adjudicated fact allow for the questions on the -- about the particular family of whom you're now inquiring?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in order to establish evidence that ethnic cleansing took place, the more that I can have people named, as is the argument over exhumations and everything else in this indictment, the better, I would have thought. Other than simply saying, I can't remember who was killed, or I can't remember, but hundreds were. He can actually name people who wer killed. And if there's another definition of ethnic cleansing, then I'd be grateful to be told what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I understand, the definition of ethnic cleansing cannot form part of the adjudicated facts. There is no such crime as ethnic cleansing. I don't think I've ever come across it. What do these specific incidents tell us? We are clearly addressing specific incidents not mentioned in the indictment. And yet Ms. Korner is questioning the witness about these. Even if we adopt the broadest possible interpretation, we cannot see them as part of the adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
